clue.text: Mother dawdles and wastes the doctor's time

parts.note: Ma is a familiar word for mother
to dawdle is to linger, hang about

explanation.surface: A mum dithers about and fritters away a GP's appointment.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who feigns illness to dodge work wastes medical time, which is exactly what shirking by pretended sickness means.

clue.text: Backbiter held, by gum

parts.note: a backbiter seems to be a slanderer and by gum a mild oath, but it is a chewing tooth at the back of the mouth held in the gums

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise that a slanderer has been arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By gum' is a northern English mild exclamation; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A rear grinding tooth bites at the back of the mouth and is anchored in the gum.

clue.text: Freedom no longer required for dogs

explanation.surface: Dogs are now free of some bureaucratic requirement.
explanation.walkthrough: The UK abolished the compulsory dog permit in 1987.
explanation.definitionFit: Licence means liberty to act, and Britain once required owners to buy an official permit for each pet dog.

clue.text: Comes close to having a listening device fitted in quarters

indicators.note: the hearing organ is placed inside the compass letters

parts.note: N and S are two of the compass quarters, north and south
the ear is the body's device for listening

explanation.surface: Getting near to having a bug installed in one's lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listening device' suggests a bug, and 'quarters' lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: Approaches, draws close: to near something is to come close to it.

clue.text: They are raised up for anyone to see

definitions.text: They are raised up for anyone to see

parts.words: They are raised up for anyone to see
parts.note: sounds like flags or banners hoisted publicly, but these are folds of skin lifted so that a person can see at all

explanation.surface: Things hoisted for public display, like flags.
explanation.definitionFit: The skin folds over the eyes must be lifted before a person can look at anything.

clue.text: Pioneer research in horticulture

explanation.surface: Early investigative study in gardening.
explanation.definitionFit: Groundwork or preliminary effort is the figurative sense; literally it is digging with a garden tool.

clue.text: Moored fleet

explanation.surface: A group of ships tied up at the quay.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat made secure is held tight to the quay, and fleet as an adjective means swift or quick.

clue.text: Didn't feel at all well

parts.note: seems to mean felt ill, but it means groped clumsily, handling something badly by touch

explanation.surface: Someone was out of sorts and felt unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: To grope or handle something clumsily is to touch it badly, so not to feel well with the hands.

clue.text: Stock old golf club for one's first course

parts.note: stock is a broth, the basis of soup
a spoon was an old wooden golf club with a lofted face

explanation.surface: Broth and an antique golf club are on hand for a starter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock' looks like supplies or shares; the definition describes what the utensil is for.
explanation.definitionFit: A rounded spoon is the utensil used for eating a starter of broth, the first course of a meal.

clue.text: Ordered security in city investment, perhaps

definitions.text: Ordered security in city investment, perhaps

parts.words: Ordered security in city investment, perhaps
parts.note: reads like a financial-pages phrase about bonds and City stocks, but investment is the military sense of besieging a town, where ordered troops seal it off

explanation.surface: A phrase about safe stocks bought in the financial City of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Security' and 'investment' look like finance; investment is also the old military word for surrounding a besieged town.
explanation.definitionFit: A military siege that cuts a town off from supplies is a form of investment in the old soldiering sense.

clue.text: Rigid habit of old king caught in affair

indicators.note: the king is caught inside the word for an affair, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: an amour is a love affair
R stands for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch of old was trapped in a dalliance by his inflexible routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' is clothing, as a nun's habit is, not a routine.
explanation.definitionFit: Habit can mean dress or garb, and a knight's metal plating is a stiff suit of clothing.

clue.text: Stubborn or eccentric characters get a hundred lines

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
ranks are lines of soldiers

explanation.surface: Obstinate oddballs are given a hundred lines as punishment at school.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsessive oddballs with fixed, peculiar notions are commonly called by this name.

clue.text: Romantic fancy brought to heel

parts.note: a fancy is a notion or idea
a ship that heels leans over, as one that lists does

explanation.surface: A lovesick whim is brought firmly under control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought to' only joins the pieces; 'heel' is the nautical sense of leaning, not the foot or obedience.
explanation.definitionFit: A romantic person is a dreamer with lofty visions, someone guided by perfect ideals.

clue.text: Switch positions to keep up maintenance

indicators.note: the two words change places, so the second word's letters are taken up and set at the front

explanation.surface: Advice to change places so as to stay on your feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Switch positions' acts on the clue's own words 'keep up', moving UP in front of KEEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Upkeep is the cost or work of keeping something in good repair, a synonym for maintenance.

clue.text: In favour of seeing prior measures made

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
vision is the faculty of seeing

explanation.surface: Supporting a look at what precautions were taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrangements made in advance for future needs are said to be made as preparations or advance measures.

clue.text: Puts order into projects

indicators.note: the words are turned into something new, reworked as a fresh arrangement of the same letters

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone organises a set of schemes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Projects' is a verb, sticks out, not a noun for schemes; the letters of PUTS and ORDER rearrange to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Juts out or sticks out beyond a surface: to project is to extend outward.

clue.text: A blooming avalanche!

parts.note: blooming sounds like a mild British curse, but it means flowering: an early white flower whose name describes a fall of snow

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry at a huge slide of snow down a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' looks like the mild British expletive; it is literal, a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: This early white spring flower's name also describes a fall of snow, the essence of an avalanche.

clue.text: Repeated invitation to adopt a more reasonable attitude

definitions.text: to adopt a more reasonable attitude

indicators.note: the invitation word is said twice over, so its letters appear two times

parts.note: come is a word of invitation, as in come in

explanation.surface: Someone is urged over and over to be sensible.
explanation.definitionFit: The doubled exclamation is a mild reproof urging someone to calm down and be more sensible.

clue.text: Give reasons that are no longer simple

parts.note: ex means former, no longer
plain means simple

explanation.surface: Justifications that have stopped being straightforward.
explanation.definitionFit: To account for something is to set out reasons, making it clear.

clue.text: Cheer a team endlessly at entry

indicators.note: the little word makes its entry into the shortened team, going inside it
the team word loses its final letter, so it has no end

parts.note: a cricket or football side is an eleven

explanation.surface: Fans cheer their side without stopping as it walks onto the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A team' is a sporting side of eleven players, as in cricket or football; 'entry' is the instruction to go inside, not a doorway.
explanation.definitionFit: To lift someone's spirits is to raise or uplift them, a sense of to cheer.

clue.text: Oriental cover for doctor in family circle

indicators.note: the doctor goes in the family word, sitting within it

parts.note: kin are one's family
MO is a medical officer, an army doctor
O is round like a circle

explanation.surface: A physician joins his relatives' social set.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose Japanese robe is an article of clothing from the Far East, so an Oriental covering.

clue.text: Teams in the market for more than a left-winger

indicators.note: the teams go inside the market word, sitting within it

parts.note: a mart is a market
an XI is a team of eleven, so teams are XIs

explanation.surface: Sides going into the market are worth more than one left-sided player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left-winger' looks like a footballer; it is political. XI is the Roman eleven, a sporting side.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Marx's communism is further to the left than a mere socialist, so more than a left-winger.

clue.text: Move to break concentration

explanation.surface: An instruction to shift oneself and disrupt someone's focus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concentration' is not mental focus but a dense gathering, as of a crowd or chemical.
explanation.definitionFit: A crowd that scatters moves away, and spreading thinly breaks up a dense mass of something.

clue.text: A clergyman has little right to come between father and son

indicators.note: the right letter must sit between the two family words, so it goes inside them

parts.note: pa is a familiar word for father
taken as written
R is the short form of right

explanation.surface: A vicar claims little right to interfere between a man and his boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A parish priest in the Church of England is commonly called by this name.

clue.text: He flies a good deal

parts.note: PI is short for pious, meaning good
a deal, as in a great deal, is a lot

explanation.surface: A man who travels by plane gets a bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A good deal' reads as a bargain, but splits into two pieces; PI for pious is a crossword convention for good.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviator is the person at the controls of an aircraft, someone who flies.

clue.text: Different from the inside or outside

indicators.note: the word the goes inside the word or, which wraps around it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something distinct from the interior or the exterior.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally: 'the' inside, 'or' outside; the word 'outside' finishes the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinct or alternative: something unlike the rest is something else.

clue.text: Tease lad about being coarse

parts.note: to rib someone is to tease them

indicators.note: the lad word is turned round, reading backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Teasing a boy about his vulgar manners.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude, bawdy humour is described as vulgar or rude, the sense of being coarse.

clue.text: OK, there's nothing left

explanation.surface: A reassurance that the cupboard is now empty.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the second half as political: with no left at all, everything is on the right.
explanation.definitionFit: Satisfactory or fine is the everyday meaning; the second sense is a joke where everything is the opposite of left.

clue.text: Unidentified girl accepts a ring

indicators.note: the girl takes in the ring, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name
O is shaped like a ring

explanation.surface: A girl says yes to an engagement ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for anonymous, an unnamed author is someone unknown.

clue.text: Observer Magazine

explanation.surface: The name of a newspaper's colour supplement.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer and The Spectator are British publications, a Sunday newspaper and a weekly political magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A watcher at an event is an onlooker, and a long-running British weekly current-affairs periodical bears this name.
